judgement.reason: It celebrates the Nativity in verse and does not say what sources linked the community to Jesus or how they came.
It shows a reconstructed worship morning, not the sources or path linking the community to Jesus.
It states the community's confession of who Jesus is.
It gives penitence as the medicine for the wounded, which answers the doubter's fear.
It affirms Jesus as God and Son of God with titles but says nothing on his relation to the Father and Spirit.
It concerns a bishop's remembered attendance at Nicaea, touching the Son's divinity only through who stood with whom.
It urges asking among brothers without quarreling, but concerns teaching and not a believer's own doubt.
It is about Christ as the foundation of faith and says nothing about inherited guilt.
It shows Ephrem reading a natural symbol for mysteries of the Son, illustrating the method but not reading Scripture.
It shows reading a pearl for many layers of meaning, an example of symbolic seeing rather than of reading Scripture.
It shows Ephrem examining a symbol and finding the Son beyond grasp, not whether Scripture was the sole authority.
It tells of Ephrem nursing the starving in a famine, not how the community responded after failing someone.
It describes Christians everywhere called by Christ's name, not whether a present-day church continues this tradition.
It shows a church building by the flood year, and the record forbids using it as evidence of what Christians did, so it says nothing of rituals.
It shows a warning given before baptism, one piece of joining, not the step-by-step process asked for.
It speaks of penitence healing spiritual wounds, which only loosely bears on an unsettled mind.
It is a written record of a lost church building, not a physical remain.
It names what candidates were warned to give up, but addresses covenant candidates, not everyone who belonged.
It touches the wedding feast only to contrast it with consecrated virgins and gives no ordinary wedding practice.
It is a flood-destruction line, not a record of worship obtained under torture.
It tells of a flood and the earliest trace of a church, not of a part of community life that unsettled us.
It shows faith as a structure rising on a foundation, which bears on how a doubter was seen but is not about the asker.
